extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what kinds of subject-matter are patentable (machines, manufactures, compositions, designs), how improvements are treated, and the unity requirement (when multiple inventions may or may not be combined in one patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle / modus operandi test for machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the alleged improved machine operates upon the same principle as the former machine; i.e., whether it produces the same effect by the same mechanical means or by means which are substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test focuses on the modus operandi, the peculiar device or manner of producing the effect. External resemblance does not determine identity of principle: "one machine may employ the same mechanical power in the same way as another machine, though the external mechanism may be apparently different. At the same time a machine may have an external resemblance to another, and yet may operate upon a different principle." If the same effect is produced, ask whether the mode of operation is substantially the same. If the effect is different, the character and importance of the effect itself is the test of a sufficient "improvement."

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a patent for an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a mere addition is made to an existing machine to produce the same effects in a better manner, the patent covers the improvement only and not the whole machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent cannot be for an effect only but for an effect produced in a given manner or by a peculiar operation. Examples: the inventor of a patent lever improved a watch but could not patent the whole watch; no patent can be obtained for abstract operations (e.g., admeasurement of time) but only for a new mode or application of machinery. If new effects are produced by an old unaltered machine, a patent for that is not legally supported. Conversely, if the principles of the machine are new, the inventor may claim the whole machine. Where an improvement overlaps a still-running earlier patent, a new patent that claims only the improvement may be valid; it comes into force after the old patent's expiration or may be used via license or purchase under the former patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to read prior specification in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action for infringement of a patent professing to be an improvement on a former patent, the specification of the former patent must be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not material whether a machine made according to the first specification would be useful or not, provided that a machine constructed according to the subsequent patent is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency test for an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is sufficient to support a patent if it contains anything material and new that is an improvement of the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted dictum of Buller J.: "if there be anything material and new, that will be an improvement of the trade, that will be sufficient to support a patent."

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'manufacture' as patent subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'manufacture' denotes anything made by the hand of man, including fabrics or substances produced by art and industry; generally a vendible article or new combination of old materials producing a new result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word has been understood to include either (a) a thing made and vendible as such (e.g., a medicine, a stove), (b) an engine or instrument employed in making articles (e.g., a stocking frame), or (c) perhaps a new process carried on by known implements producing a better/cheaper result. The best general definition: any new combination of old materials constituting a new result or production in the form of a vendible article (not being machinery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'manufacture' and 'machine' (how to classify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify an article as a manufacture if produced and intended to be sold and used separately and its merit is the article itself (better or cheaper); classify as a machine if its merit appears only after incorporation with mechanism and produces a new effect when combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction may require discrimination but is not vital for patent validity: if the thing is correctly described, novel and useful, and meets statutory requisites, it may be left to general interpretation whether it is a machine or manufacture. If intended as a merchantable commodity sold separately, treat as manufacture; if its merit arises only in combination with mechanism, treat as machine or an improvement of an existing machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter – test of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions of matter (medicines, compositions used in the arts) are patentable; the test of novelty is whether the combination is new, not whether the individual materials are new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee produces a composition by different proportions of the same ingredients, or by the same and other ingredients, the patent may be good. The patentee is not confined to the precise ingredients provided the different combinations he uses are equally new. The patent may cover both the composition itself and the process of making it where both are new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents and their scope
rubrics_metrics.description: New and original designs for manufactures, prints/patterns on fabrics, busts/statues, ornaments, shapes/configurations of articles of manufacture are patentable under a statute (seven-year term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These patents relate to forms impressed upon material and marks adopted by tradesmen; they occupy a middle ground between copyright and patents. Identity between two forms is judged by principles akin to colorable imitation: exact resemblance not required to find imitation; these principles are more frequently applied in copyright but also relevant to design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the subject-matter (statutory singularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents statutes require the subject-matter of a patent to be one invention or discovery (singular), so generally two distinct and independent inventions with no necessary connection cannot be united in one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: (1) statute language speaks of 'an invention' not 'inventions'; (2) practical inconvenience and risk that if part is not original the whole patent may be void. Determination of unity often depends on the object the inventor proposes to accomplish.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple inventions can constitute one subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Several distinct inventions or machines may form one subject-matter if the inventor has brought them together for a purpose which can only be effected by their union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the collection is combined to achieve a single unified purpose, the patent may legitimately claim the union as one subject-matter. By contrast, if the patent claims both the combination and also distinct independent purposes which each invention can effect by itself, then multiple subject-matters are embraced and the patent is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of claiming parts and combination (coverage of parts vs combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee describes several distinct and independent parts intended to be used in combination and is the first inventor of each, the patent covers all the parts and the combination; use of any one part by another is infringement. But if the inventor is not the original inventor of the several things and the combination itself is the subject-matter, use of parts not amounting to the same combination is not infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus whether a patentee may enforce against use of individual parts depends on whether he was the original inventor of those parts or whether his invention is limited to the combination only. The specification's accuracy and distinctness in stating particulars of the invention materially affect the scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting several improvements on the same machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be taken for several improvements on one and the same machine, or for two machines invented by the patentee which conduce to the same common purpose and object, even if they are capable of distinct use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a patent cannot be taken for two distinct machines designed for totally distinct and independent objects. If the patent is for an improved machine incorporating several distinct improvements and any one improvement is pirated, the patentee may have a remedy because the patent includes those specified improvements. Conversely, if the patent is only for a new combination, and not for particular improvements, merely using parts of the machinery will not infringe unless the combination itself is substantially violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of accurate and distinct specification; claiming beyond invention voids patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is confined to the particulars and summary of the invention stated in the specification; if the patent covers particulars that are not new, the patent is void even if those particulars are slight or of little importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscure language in a specification makes it difficult to ascertain the nature and extent of the invention claimed. Courts cannot reject a claim that appears in the specification; if included and found not to be new the whole patent may be invalid. The patentee cannot later expand beyond the scope he summed up as his invention.
